Although the Firmamend Arbiter was once the centerpiece of faith among the intellectuals and merchants, the Aeon was one typically indifferent to the lives of mortals. Compared to that Arbiter's worldview, the people of Xianzhou leaned more toward pragmatism when it comes to their preferred spirituality. Therefore, diverse choices of new beliefs bloomed among them.

Quite a number of people went against the trend and became faithfuls of the Yaoshi. They firmly believed that the behavior of the Denizens of Abundance deviated from Yaoshi's will, and the mara-struck only existed because Yaoshi's will was improperly executed. These people called themselves Disciples of Sanctus Medicus (hereafter referred to as the "Old Disciples of Sanctus Medicus" to differentiate them from modern terrorists).

For a long time in history, the Old Disciples of Sanctus Medicus were not a notorious group. They accepted skepticism with an open mind and built apothecaries to help the poor and needy. For those who had long abandoned Yaoshi beliefs, the behavior of the group was pathetic and laughable, though not particularly detestable.

Here is something worth mentioning, though the Xianzhou people spared no efforts to diminish it: The predecessor of the Cold Springs Sect, which overhauled the entire Xianzhou healthcare system and stepped onto the historical stage several millennia after the Crisis of Belief, was the Old Disciples of Sanctus Medicus that existed in secret for thousands of years. In recent years, a group of sorcerers wreaked havoc by impersonating the Disciples of Sanctus Medicus. Only then did the Cold Springs Sect publish a statement to clarify that they had abandoned the erroneous belief in the Plagues Author.

Many intellectuals abandoned their old paths for good and chose to follow the Wisdomwalker on the Path of Erudition. They were called the Wisdom Sect. Back then, most Wisdom Sect members preferred to focus on academic research in their ivory towers than spending time on secular matters. Hence, their presence was not felt much during the Crisis of Belief era when the people were spoiled with a plethora of selectable beliefs. (They continued to use the term, "the Sacrosancts," mostly because they attached little importance to the title of Aeons.)

The Wisdom Sect still exists, although it is hardly know and only has a small group of followers left. The Wisdom Sapientia Academe in the Yuque, which dates back to <unbreak>5,000</unbreak> years ago, has provided a constant supply of talented technicians who believe in the Wisdomwalker to various Xianzhou commissions. Not a single Xianzhou person who believes in the Reignbow Arbiter has any issues with the arrangement.

After all, to most Xianzhou people of sane and pragmatic mind, The Hunt is a righteous path to follow, not a shackle that controls the people. As long as you walk the right path, the Aeon you believe in is just something that helps you achieve your goals.

Amid cheers, silks, delicacies, and jewels rained onto the platform, forming a small mountain. "Shun the Chrysos Heirs' raving lies. Have faith in Kephale. So long as we pray earnestly, the god shall deliver salvation..." She pushed her way through the crowd, losing the bread in her hand somewhere along the way. Desperately, she looked around, only to find condescending faces staring down at her, surging toward her like a restless tide. Her knees went weak as mocking glances and threatening smiles blurred before her eyes. But the distant voices had already burrowed into her ears, and she couldn't stop. "Thief!" "Criminal!" "Wretch!" Closing her eyes, she plunged from that three-hundred-meter-high wall. "So... hungry..." Icy waters swallowed her consciousness. Analysis Target In the artwork Moonlit Stars, eleven celestial bodies are scattered at irregular intervals, forming a vast spiral nebula. Approaching this from the angle of deconstructing its core motif, I must determine: "Why is it called 'art'?" This is to say, breaking it down into a collection of quantifiable parameters. II. Compositional Analysis The artwork has a semi-matte finish with faintly visible, wave-like brushstroke textures. The color layers are rich and complex. The white is not pure white. Rather, it is composed of densely layered point-like particles: 1.3% cool gray, 2.1% cobalt blue, and more, replicating the optically deep hues of a starry night. ... Replicating these brushstrokes would not be difficult. With that in mind, I have decided to conduct an experiment. III. Replication Experiment Faithful replication of the data should yield an artistic result identical to the original. Through an astronomical number of floating-point calculations, I am certain: Every pixel reflects the original appearance of Moonlit Stars with a margin of error no greater than 0.1%. But when I invited the survivors of Moonlit Stars' homeland — Moonshield — to view the painting, they studied it for a long moment before an expression of confusion crossed their faces. "There's something missing, I think..." "This painting shows the sky above my homeland, but I can't feel its warmth..." ... On a sensory level, the observers could recognize the visual similarity between the two paintings, yet all agreed that the copy "lacked warmth." I revisited the background materials on the original: Moonlit Stars was painted after the artist's world had perished, a vision of their homeland drawn entirely from memory. Their work was not an objective reconstruction, but an emotionally infused reinterpretation. "You reproduced the image, but you never understood the painter or the world they depicted." — A critique from the viewers. IV. Conclusion If "art" exists within quantifiable data, then my duplication should be equivalent, yet viewer feedback has refuted this hypothesis. I will continue to explore the motif. This report has, at the very least, ruled out one incorrect answer. I believe this marks the beginning of "understanding."
